Chapter Two: Examining Internalized Beliefs and Everyday Complicity
Now that we've set the stage, it's time to turn inward—really taking a look at the beliefs, habits, and assumptions we've picked up along the way. This isn't about blaming yourself. Think of it more like taking an honest, gentle inventory. We're exploring how white supremacy might have shaped parts of our thinking, our feelings, and even our everyday behavior—often without us even realizing it.
So, what exactly is internalized white supremacy? It's when the messages society sends about race—things we hear from family, see in the media, learn at school, or just absorb from the culture—slowly become part of how we see the world. They can sneak in as subtle preferences, little unspoken fears, or those snap judgments we make without even thinking. Maybe you notice you feel a bit safer around people who look like you, or you catch yourself thinking certain neighborhoods are "better," but you haven't really stopped to ask why.
Another big idea to sit with is complicity. This means realizing that just benefiting from an unfair system—even if you never asked for those benefits—helps keep it going. It doesn't mean every single thing you do is harmful, but it does mean that staying quiet or doing nothing can allow these patterns to stick around. Ever laughed at a racist joke just to avoid an awkward moment, or stayed silent when someone was being treated unfairly? That's complicity in action.
To put it another way, imagine a river that's polluted way upstream. Even if you live downstream and never add to the pollution, you're still drinking that water. You're affected by what's in it. In the same way, living in a society shaped by white supremacy means everyone is touched by it—even if they're not actively making it worse.
So, how do we start this honest self-reflection? Here are a few questions you might ask yourself:
When have I benefited from being part of the dominant group, even if I didn't ask for it?
What stereotypes or assumptions might I have picked up about people of other races?
And how have I reacted when I've seen racism happening around me?
There are some practical ways to dig a little deeper here, too.
Try journaling about your own experiences with race and privilege, especially those moments that felt uncomfortable or confusing.
Pay attention to who's included—and who's left out—in your social circles, at work, or in the things you watch and read.
And maybe most importantly, be open to feedback. If someone calls you in or points out something you've said or done that's hurtful, especially if they're a person of color, see if you can listen without getting defensive. It's tough, but it's how we grow.
Remember, this isn't about getting it perfect. It's about making progress, one step at a time. The more we build our self-awareness, the more we can catch those old automatic reactions—and start making conscious, thoughtful choices instead.
Ultimately, the goal is to move from being a passive bystander to taking active responsibility. Because, as small as they might seem, those everyday actions really do matter.
